justification: Documentation-only PR — seven markdown files in docs/pitch/. No served output, no data path, no user-facing UI. Standard tier is the right ceiling; Critical is reserved for served outputs and Basic would skip the grounding gate this report needs to survive the same doc-claim checks these files preach.

No new files were referenced without opening the target.

Mitigation: every PR number in cheat-sheet.md was verified by `git log --all --oneline --diff-filter=A -- scripts/<file>.py` (falsifiability #890, doc_claims #890, lint_fabricated_verdicts #859, liability_language #835, validate_schema_contract #856, qa_gate #835, lint_hardcoded_confidence #872). Every PR cited in the rehearsal (#886, #859, #890, #856) is a real PR in the log and was cited for what it actually did.

Prior-art sweep for pitch/positioning material: ~/.claude/plans/*pitch*, docs/PITCH*, docs/*pitch* — no hits (verified during the four-sweep before writing). ce-linkedin-rewrite-2026-06.md exists but is quarantined per STRATEGY_REVIEW_2026-08-08.md §10 — its product claims predate the truth-in-claims campaign and are not reused here.

functions.name: runbook demo driver (heredoc, not a tracked file)
functions.input: the runbook's own two heredocs — one five-line dummy, one twenty-line driver — plus scripts/falsifiability.py copied into cwd by the setup step
functions.output: stdout — five labelled lines with sha256 prefixes and rc codes; exit 0 on success
functions.if_none: If scripts/falsifiability.py is missing, ImportError before any plant runs — the setup section names this explicitly and gives the cp command. If the dummy file was not created by step 1, PlantDidNotTake is raised with a clear message before the block body runs. The runbook's 'what can go wrong' table lists both.

falsifiable_check.fails_when: The demo prints 'bytes identical to baseline?  False' — the plant-restore harness left the file mutated on disk. Also fails if the planted rc is not non-zero (the check didn't catch the lie). Both were verified to go the right way during writing; both directions were exercised (baseline rc=0, planted rc=1, restored rc=0, sha256 restored to a1ea58c8278f, matching baseline).

break_it.scenario: The demo runbook is executed on a laptop where the buyer's Python has assertions disabled (PYTHONOPTIMIZE=1) — the planted 'a - b' would not raise, the check would stay green, and the runbook's central claim ('non-zero means the lie was caught') would be visibly false in front of the buyer.
break_it.what_happens: Lawrence delivers a demo that contradicts what he just said it would do; every subsequent claim in the pitch loses credibility.
break_it.how: docs/pitch/demo-runbook.md:117-118 — the 'what can go wrong' table names PYTHONOPTIMIZE as a specific cause and instructs Lawrence to bail out verbally ('let me not fake this, my machine at home just showed it going red — happy to send you the recording') rather than talk past it. This is the one failure mode where the honest response is more valuable than the demo working.
break_it.repro: PYTHONOPTIMIZE=1 python3 demo.py in the scratch directory; check that the planted rc is 0 rather than 1; confirm the runbook tells Lawrence what to say.

break_it.scenario: A hostile buyer reads positioning-paragraph.md Version A, files Lawrence as 'AI prompter', and follows up with Q6 in rehearsal.md: 'So you're really a prompt engineer, not an engineer.' Version A alone (without the rehearsal answer to that specific trap) leaves Lawrence one clarifying sentence short.
break_it.what_happens: Buyer disengages mentally between Q1 and Q6, and Lawrence loses the room before he gets to the demo.
break_it.how: docs/pitch/positioning-paragraph.md:16-45 ships TWO versions with an explicit selection rule ('If the room is engineering-heavy, switch to B') and B's opening — 'a rule I hadn't seen written down elsewhere: before I trust a check, I break the code underneath it and prove the check goes red' — is a specific technical claim a prompt engineer would not make. rehearsal.md Q6:98-116 handles the trap directly with 'if your view is that a person who directs an AI is not doing engineering, then this isn't a fit and we should end the call.'
break_it.repro: Read Version A aloud to an engineer, then ask them Q6's trap. Read Version B to a second engineer, then ask them the same trap. Version B is more robust standalone. See §Positioning-trap-test in this report below.

break_it.scenario: A buyer or hostile reviewer picks up the cheat-sheet, clicks PR #890, and finds a PR that does not contain scripts/falsifiability.py — the entire 'every claim references something on GitHub' promise collapses on the first click.
break_it.what_happens: Every artefact loses credibility in one click.
break_it.how: Every PR number in cheat-sheet.md was verified during writing via `git log --all --oneline --diff-filter=A -- scripts/<file>.py`. The commit-history block from the earlier scratch is captured in the transcript; PRs shown are the ones that ADD each file, not later commits that touched it.
break_it.repro: For each of the 7 rows in cheat-sheet.md, run `git log --all --oneline --diff-filter=A -- <script-path>` and confirm the cited PR number appears in the head commit's subject line.

break_it.scenario: A buyer asks Lawrence to run the demo on their code and their code is not Python — Lawrence has said 'the same harness runs on any Python file' but their product is Rust / Go / TypeScript.
break_it.what_happens: Lawrence backs off a claim in front of the buyer, or accepts an engagement he can't reproduce the demo inside.
break_it.how: docs/pitch/demo-runbook.md:135-138 says explicitly: 'It doesn't say every check on my repo works this way. Only the reliability findings that made it into the last twenty-plus PRs use this discipline.' docs/pitch/qualifying-diagnostic.md is language-agnostic — Q1/Q2/Q3 don't require Python; Probe 1 (marketing-page grep) and Probe 2 (public-endpoint diff) both run against any product. The pitch package as a whole works for non-Python codebases; the specific plant-restore demo does not, and the runbook is explicit that the demo is for the meeting, not the engagement.
break_it.repro: N/A — the mitigation is in what the artefacts do not claim.

break_it.scenario: The four PR numbers cited in rehearsal.md (#886, #859, #890, #856) do not describe the specific finding Lawrence claims in the answer.
break_it.what_happens: First serious buyer clicks the PR mid-call, contradicts Lawrence live, meeting ends.
break_it.how: Each PR number was cross-checked against git log: #886 c6d64ed 'feat(shadow): remove the adjacent-lot construction check from the product' — the 538-attempts-zero-results finding, correctly claimed; #859 2ed1687 'feat(gates): fabricated-verdict lint' — the DQ-36 finding, correctly claimed; #890 f5acb08 'chore(gates): a shared plant-restore harness' — the design decisions Lawrence claims (fail-closed, sidecar shell-search, hook not test) all appear in the falsifiability.py module docstring; #856 8260f6b 'chore(gates): schema-contract check, first CI workflow, and the live defect it found' — the '4,000+ tests all green through a table rename' finding is exactly this PR's story.
break_it.repro: For each PR number in rehearsal.md, `git log --all --oneline | grep '#<n>'` and read the commit subject aloud; check it matches what the rehearsal answer promises.

positioning_trap_test.question_run: Does Version A of docs/pitch/positioning-paragraph.md survive Q6's trap ('So you're really a prompt engineer, not an engineer.') without needing the rehearsal follow-up to save it?
positioning_trap_test.verdict: Version A does not survive standalone. Its strongest specific claim ('designed the checks that catch each class of silent failure') is generic enough that a hostile reader can dismiss it. Version B does survive standalone: 'a rule I hadn't seen written down elsewhere: before I trust a check, I break the code underneath it and prove the check goes red' is a specific technique with a stated novelty claim, which a prompt engineer would not phrase that way.
positioning_trap_test.recommendation: Memorise Version B first for standalone survival; keep Version A for warmer buyer contexts where undersell is more damaging than over-modesty. If Lawrence has bandwidth for only one paragraph on the first pitch, Version B is the safer choice.
